title: A Man Cursed King David to His Face—and David Refused to Let His Soldiers Kill Him
paragraphs:
A Man Cursed King David to His Face—and David Refused to Let His Soldiers Kill Him
He threw stones at the king, called him a murderer, and humiliated him in front of everyone. David had enough armed men to silence him in seconds. Instead, the fallen king said something that exposes what may be hiding inside all of us.
There are moments when you discover who you really are.
Not when people applaud you.
Not when everything is working.
Not when your prayers seem answered, your family is peaceful, your reputation is intact, and everyone around you agrees that God is blessing your life.
You discover something much deeper about yourself when you are wounded...
and someone decides to throw another stone.
That is where David was.
Not sitting securely on the throne.
Not standing over Goliath with Israel shouting his name.
Not carrying the giant’s severed head while people celebrated the shepherd boy who trusted God.
This David was running.
His own son Absalom had turned against him.
The conspiracy had grown.
Jerusalem was slipping from his hands.
Men who once honored him were choosing sides.
David—the king, warrior, psalmist, giant-killer—was leaving Jerusalem in humiliation.
And then came Shimei.
Sometimes the cruelest voices do not arrive when you are strong.
They wait until you are bleeding.
Second Samuel 16:5 tells us that as David approached Bahurim, Shimei son of Gera came out from the family of Saul and began cursing him.
He did not merely mutter under his breath.
He followed David and his men.
He cursed.
He threw stones.
He kicked dust into the air.
Imagine the scene.
David is surrounded by warriors, mighty men who have spilled blood on battlefields. Yet this man walks along the hillside hurling insults and stones at Israel’s king.
And Shimei knows exactly where to strike.
He attacks David’s past.
He essentially calls him a man of blood.
A worthless man.
He interprets David’s catastrophe as divine judgment and tells him that his kingdom has collapsed because God is paying him back.
There is something especially painful about being attacked with a version of your own history.
Because David really did have blood in his past.
Uriah was dead.
Bathsheba had been taken.
David had committed adultery.
He had manipulated circumstances surrounding Uriah’s death.
The prophet Nathan had confronted him.
David had confessed, “I have sinned against the LORD” (2 Samuel 12:13).
And although God forgave David, forgiveness did not mean that every earthly consequence disappeared.
That is what makes Shimei’s accusations so psychologically brutal.
They were not entirely disconnected from David’s shame.
Have you ever been forgiven by God...
but someone still knew where the grave was buried?
Have you ever repented of something, yet a person kept resurrecting the version of you that Christ was changing?
Have you ever heard words that hurt so badly because somewhere inside you whispered:
“What if I deserve this?”
Then you understand something about that road to Bahurim.
Shimei kept cursing.
And one of David’s warriors had heard enough.
Abishai, son of Zeruiah, said to the king:
“Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go over and take off his head.”
That was not metaphorical.
Abishai wanted Shimei dead.
One command from David...
and the cursing would stop.
One nod.
One sword.
Silence.
And here is where the story becomes dangerous for anyone who has ever fantasized about making somebody pay.
David refused.
The Hebrew of his response deserves attention.
David says:
כִּי יְקַלֵּל וְכִי יְהוָה אָמַר לוֹ קַלֵּל אֶת־דָּוִד
Ki yeqallel, vekhi YHWH amar lo, qallel et-David...
The sense is:
“If he is cursing because the LORD has said to him, ‘Curse David’...”
Then David asks, in effect:
Who can demand, “Why have you done this?”
David was not declaring that every accusation Shimei made was true.
He was not establishing a doctrine that every abusive voice speaks for God.
He was not telling victims that cruelty should always be tolerated.
And he certainly was not declaring Shimei morally innocent.
David was doing something far more searching.
He was acknowledging the sovereignty of God even while he was being humiliated.
He refused to seize vengeance merely because vengeance was within reach.
That distinction matters.
Biblical surrender is not pretending evil is good.
Biblical forgiveness is not calling abuse holy.
Biblical humility is not saying lies are true.
And trusting God with justice does not mean justice ceases to matter.
It means you refuse to become your own god in order to obtain it.
David could have killed Shimei.
Instead, David looked beyond Shimei.
That is extraordinary.
Most of us stare at the stone.
David looked toward God.
Most of us obsess over the person throwing dirt.
David wondered what God might be doing in the dust.
Then David said something heartbreaking.
His own son was trying to kill him.
Why, then, should he be shocked that a Benjaminite cursed him?
And then comes the sentence that changes the emotional temperature of the entire scene:
אוּלַי יִרְאֶה יְהוָה בְּעֵינִי
Ulay yir’eh YHWH be‘eini...
“Perhaps the LORD will look upon my affliction...”
David does not know how this ends.
Read that again.
He does not know.
There is no triumphant soundtrack playing behind him.
No prophet steps out and announces that everything will be restored by sunset.
David is walking through humiliation while Shimei continues cursing him.
And all David has is...
perhaps.
“Perhaps the LORD will look upon my affliction...”
Perhaps God sees.
Perhaps God has not abandoned me.
Perhaps God can bring good even out of this.
Perhaps mercy is still possible.
Somebody reading this knows exactly what it feels like to live inside that word.
Perhaps.
Perhaps my marriage can still heal.
Perhaps my child will come home.
Perhaps God can restore what my sin damaged.
Perhaps Jesus can still use me after what I did.
Perhaps I am not beyond redemption.
Perhaps the chapter everybody thinks destroyed me is not the chapter where God stops writing.
And this is where David’s road points beyond David.
Because centuries later, another King would be rejected.
Another Son of David would walk a road of humiliation.
Another King would be mocked.
Another King would be falsely accused.
Another King would have insults thrown at Him.
Another King would possess the power to destroy His enemies...
and refuse to use that power to escape the suffering before Him.
Jesus Christ.
At His arrest, Jesus said that He could appeal to His Father and receive more than twelve legions of angels (Matthew 26:53).
Think about that.
Calvary did not happen because Jesus lacked power.
The cross happened while infinite power was being restrained by infinite love.
They mocked Him.
He stayed.
They struck Him.
He stayed.
They drove nails through Him.
He stayed.
And while hanging between heaven and earth, Jesus prayed:
“Father, forgive them...”
David spared the man who cursed him.
Jesus went infinitely further.
Jesus gave Himself for sinners who had rebelled against God.
That includes us.
The scandal of the Gospel is not merely that wicked people can be forgiven.
The scandal is that forgiveness came at the cost of the blood of the innocent Son of God.
You and I are not merely David in this story.
Sometimes we are Shimei.
We have thrown our own rebellion toward the King.
Maybe not with literal stones.
But with sin.
Pride.
Lust.
Bitterness.
Secret compromise.
Self-righteousness.
Gossip.
Hatred.
Religious performance without surrender.
We wanted God’s gifts while resisting His authority.
We wanted grace without repentance.
Heaven without holiness.
A Savior without a Lord.
And yet Jesus did not come merely to crush rebels.
He came to save sinners.
The King we offended became the sacrifice for our sin.
That is grace.
Not God pretending sin does not matter.
The cross proves that sin matters more terribly than we like to admit.
Grace means the judgment our sin deserved was borne by Christ for everyone who comes to Him in repentant faith.
Jesus does not simply improve your public image.
He raises spiritually dead people to life.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He transforms.
He rewrites stories.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But there is another uncomfortable question hiding on that dusty road.
Who is your Shimei?
Whose name immediately entered your mind?
Who embarrassed you?
Who betrayed you?
Who keeps reminding people of what you did?
Who misunderstood you?
Who posted something about you?
Who walked away?
Who said the thing you still replay at 2:00 in the morning?
Who made you want to reach for your own version of Abishai’s sword?
Maybe your sword is not steel.
Maybe it is a Facebook post.
A screenshot.
A rumor.
A perfectly crafted message designed to wound them exactly where you know they are vulnerable.
Maybe your sword is silence used as punishment.
Maybe it is public humiliation.
Maybe it is telling everybody your side until their reputation is buried beneath it.
Maybe you keep saying, “I just want the truth known.”
But somewhere beneath the truth...
you want blood.
David’s restraint asks a terrifying question:
What if victory is not getting the last word?
What if sometimes victory is having the power to retaliate...
and placing the sword back into its sheath?
That does not mean refusing appropriate boundaries.
It does not mean remaining in danger.
It does not mean concealing crimes, protecting abusers, rejecting lawful justice, or pretending wrongdoing never happened.
Scripture does not require us to call darkness light.
But there is a difference between pursuing what is right and feeding revenge.
Romans 12:19 tells believers not to avenge themselves, but to leave room for the judgment of God.
Why?
Because vengeance makes a terrible god out of a wounded human heart.
And wounded hearts are rarely satisfied with “enough.”
We want the other person to feel what we felt.
Then a little more.
And another little more.
Until somewhere along the road, while punishing the person who wounded us...
we become someone we never intended to become.
David refused that road.
But do not romanticize him.
This is the same David who had failed catastrophically.
That is part of the beauty.
The man showing restraint here is not a flawless saint.
He is a broken man.
A disciplined man.
A forgiven man living amid consequences.
A man who has learned that possessing power does not mean you have permission to use it however your emotions demand.
Maybe that is why this story hurts.
Some lessons can only be learned after we have been shattered.
Sometimes the person who once abused power becomes the person who finally understands restraint.
Sometimes the person who desperately needed mercy becomes slower to deny mercy to somebody else.
And maybe you are standing somewhere on that road right now.
Stones are flying.
Dust is in your eyes.
Your reputation feels bruised.
Your past is screaming.
And the sword is within reach.
Before you swing...
look toward Jesus.
Not because what happened to you was insignificant.
Not because the person who wounded you was necessarily right.
Not because justice does not matter.
Look toward Jesus because bitterness cannot resurrect you.
Revenge cannot cleanse you.
Winning the argument cannot heal the deepest wound in you.
Only Christ can reach that far.
Maybe the real battle is not between you and the person throwing stones.
Maybe the battle is over what their stones are turning you into.
Do not let somebody else’s sin disciple your heart.
Do not let their cruelty teach you cruelty.
Do not let their hatred decide who you become.
Bring the wound to Christ.
Bring the rage.
Bring the humiliation.
Bring the fantasies of revenge you would never admit in church.
Bring the screenshots.
Bring the memory.
Bring the name.
Jesus already knows.
Repent where you have sinned.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Seek justice where justice is appropriate.
Establish wise boundaries where they are necessary.
But do not worship vengeance.
And if you have been Shimei...
if you have been the one throwing stones...
repent.
Stop defending it.
Stop dressing cruelty in spiritual language.
Stop calling gossip “discernment.”
Stop calling hatred “truth.”
Stop using another person’s genuine failures as permission to enjoy destroying them.
Jesus did not die so we could become religious experts at throwing stones.
He died to reconcile sinners to God and create a people transformed by grace.
Maybe this exposed something you have been hiding.
Be honest.
There may be another believer reading your words who needs to discover they are not the only Christian still fighting this battle.
And if someone came to your mind while reading this, do not weaponize the article against them.
Pray first.
Then, if sharing it would genuinely help rather than shame them, send it with love.
We do not purchase favor with Him. Grace cannot be bought.
You need Jesus.
Not merchandise.
Not an inspirational quote.
Not religious appearance.
Jesus.
The crucified and risen King.
The Savior who receives repentant sinners.
The Lord who can take the ugliest chapter of your life and refuse to let it become the title of your story.
David walked while Shimei cursed.
Stone after stone.
Insult after insult.
Dust rising around him.
And David refused to answer every stone with a sword.
Maybe that is the word someone desperately needs tonight.
You do not have to destroy everyone who reminds you of your wounds.
You do not have to win every battle your pride volunteers you for.
You do not have to rewrite your past by yourself.
There is already a King who walked through humiliation.
A King who endured the cross.
A King who entered the grave.
A King who rose again.
And when Jesus takes hold of a surrendered life, even the chapters covered in dust, blood, regret, betrayal, and shame are no longer beyond redemption.
So when the stones start flying again...
remember who is holding the pen.
Your wound may explain why you reached for the sword—but Jesus can teach your scarred hand how to let it go.
